content: Diflunisal is a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) that may increase the risk of heart attack or stroke, particularly in individuals who take it for extended periods. These events can occur without warning and may be fatal. Inform your doctor if you or your family have a history of heart disease, heart attack, or stroke, if you smoke, or if you have high cholesterol, high blood pressure, or diabetes. Seek emergency medical attention if you experience chest pain, shortness of breath, weakness on one side of the body, or slurred speech. Avoid taking diflunisal immediately before or after coronary artery bypass graft (CABG) surgery. Diflunisal and other NSAIDs can cause ulcers, bleeding, or perforations in the stomach or intestines, which may occur at any time during treatment, often without warning, and can be fatal. The risk is higher for individuals who take NSAIDs long-term, are older, in poor health, or consume large amounts of alcohol. Notify your doctor if you are taking anticoagulants (e.g., warfarin), aspirin, other NSAIDs (e.g., ibuprofen, naproxen), or oral steroids (e.g., dexamethasone, prednisone). Also, inform your doctor if you have a history of ulcers, gastrointestinal bleeding, or other bleeding disorders. Stop taking diflunisal and contact your doctor if you experience stomach pain, heartburn, vomiting blood or material resembling coffee grounds, blood in the stool, or black, tarry stools. Take diflunisal as prescribed, usually every 8-12 hours with water, milk, or food. Swallow the tablets whole without splitting, chewing, or crushing them. It may take several days or longer to feel the full benefits of the medication. Continue taking it as directed by your doctor, even if you feel well. Do not take more or less than prescribed. Before starting diflunisal, inform your doctor if you are allergic to it, aspirin, other NSAIDs, or any other medications. Provide a complete list of all prescription and nonprescription medications, vitamins, and supplements you are taking. Mention any conditions such as asthma, nasal polyps, swelling in the extremities, or liver or kidney disease. If you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding, inform your doctor. Do not take diflunisal if you suspect you have a viral infection, such as chickenpox or the flu, and do not give it to children with viral illnesses. Store diflunisal in its original container, tightly closed, at room temperature, away from heat and moisture. Dispose of expired or unused medication properly, consulting your pharmacist for guidance. In case of overdose, contact a poison control center or emergency services immediately. Symptoms of overdose may include drowsiness, vomiting, upset stomach, diarrhea, decreased urination, rapid breathing, fast heartbeat, sweating, ringing in the ears, confusion, or loss of consciousness. Diflunisal may cause minor side effects such as vomiting, diarrhea, constipation, gas, headache, dizziness, ringing in the ears, or vision problems. Notify your doctor if these symptoms persist or worsen. Serious side effects include stomach upset, unusual bleeding or bruising, yellowing of the skin or eyes, rash, fever, chills, swelling, difficulty breathing, or unexplained weight gain. Stop taking the medication and contact your doctor immediately if you experience any severe side effects. Always read the medication guide provided by your pharmacist and consult your doctor or pharmacist with any questions. Do not share this medication with others, and inform laboratory personnel that you are taking diflunisal before undergoing any tests.
